fields.rationale: States cluster around whether they require ECFMG certification alone, ECFMG plus postgraduate training (1–2 yrs), extended postgraduate training (3+ yrs), special alternative pathways (Fifth Pathway, faculty, English fluency, employment restrictions), or leave requirements largely to board discretion.

assignments.raw_value: Foreign medical graduates must complete three years of postgraduate training (or other requirements establishing proof of competency as determined by the board), pass examinations as specified by the board, and meet all other requirements including pain management and opioid use and addiction education

Foreign medical graduates must be graduates of medical schools accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education, Commission on Osteopathic College Accreditation, or listed in the International Medical Education Directory or equivalent, and must pass USMLE or COMLEX-USA within three attempts.

Foreign medical school graduates must have entrance requirements and course of instruction approved by the Arkansas State Medical Board; must serve 3 years in postgraduate medical education program outside the United States, complete all steps of USMLE, obtain ECFMG certification, and either complete 1+ year of ACGME-accredited fellowship training or receive ABMS certification

Foreign medical graduates must hold a standard certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates, complete a fifth pathway program, or serve as a full-time assistant professor or higher at an approved school of medicine for 36 months

International medical graduates must complete one year of postgraduate clinical training approved by the board. If the international medical school is not an approved medical college, the applicant is eligible for licensure at the board's discretion if they meet all other requirements and hold current specialty board certification from the American Board of Medical Specialties or American Osteopathic Association

Foreign medical graduates must have received the degree of doctor of medicine, osteopathic medicine or its equivalent, satisfied educational requirements specified in regulations, and either successfully completed all components of a fifth pathway program conducted by an American medical school accredited by the American Medical Association or American Osteopathic Association, or received certification from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates

Foreign medical graduates from schools listed in IMED must pass the ECFMG and FSMB examinations. Graduates from schools not listed in IMED must complete 3 years of ACGME-approved postgraduate residency training and pass the ECFMG and FSMB examinations. All foreign graduates must provide documentary proof that U.S./Canadian clinical rotations were conducted at accredited institutions.

Foreign medical school graduates must have credentials evaluated by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG), hold active ECFMG certificate, pass ECFMG examination, and complete approved residency of at least 1-2 years depending on school certification status

Graduates of non-board-approved foreign medical schools who graduated after July 1, 1985 must complete three years of ACGME/AOA/board-approved residency, fellowship, or postgraduate training; must pass ECFMG qualifying examination; aliens must have resided in the United States for one year (except Canadian medical school graduates)

Foreign medical school graduates must have at least two years of residency in an accredited program and hold the national certificate of the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or pass the Medical Council of Canada Evaluating Examination, or hold the Fifth Pathway Program certificate

Foreign medical graduates must hold a valid standard certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or similar accrediting agency, and must complete two years of postgraduate training instead of one.

International physicians must meet specific requirements including graduation from an international medical program, post-graduate medical training, practice in home country for at least 3 years or 500 hours clinical experience in the United States, practice within the last 5 years or waiver, and basic English fluency demonstrated by passing occupational English test for medicine or equivalent exam approved by the board

International medical graduates must have education certified by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates, pass USMLE Steps 1, 2 CK, and 3, maintain unencumbered license from another country, and not be licensed in any US state or territory

Foreign medical graduates must complete minimum of two (2) years of postgraduate training in a hospital or institution located in the United States or Canada which meets standards approved by nationally recognized medical or osteopathic accrediting bodies, or the board may waive the second year.
Foreign medical graduates must pass an examination given by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG)

Foreign medical graduates must be certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or by an approved United States specialty board, and must complete a prescribed course of postgraduate training

International medical graduates must have completed a residency or substantially similar post-graduate medical training in their licensing country or practiced as a medical professional for at least five years, be in good standing with their licensing country's medical institution, possess basic fluency in English, and have an offer for employment at a hospital-licensed facility. They must provide medical services only at hospital-licensed facilities for two years from original licensure.

Foreign medical school graduates must be certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or its successor, pass a qualifying examination for foreign medical school graduates, and complete 2 years of postgraduate medical education training or successfully complete a fifth pathway program followed by 2 years of postgraduate training
Foreign medical graduates must meet same examination and educational requirements as domestic graduates; ECFMG certification may be required by board rule

Foreign medical school graduates approved by the National Educational Council for Foreign Medical Graduates may obtain a limited institutional license for practice in state institutions; must meet minimum standards of qualifications including moral, experience and proficiency; limited to one year renewable annually; may not hold such license longer than five years unless waived by the board; must eventually obtain regular licensure or the board may refuse to renew
Foreign medical graduates must pass the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates examination or equivalent

Foreign medical graduates must present evidence of degree, 24 months of postgraduate training in US/Canada, ECFMG certificate, and English language proficiency. Board has discretion to accept alternative qualifications.

Foreign medical graduates must provide a permanent certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or credentials certifying passage of the Visa Qualifying Examination, or credentials certifying completion of the Fifth Pathway program and ECFMG examination. Foreign medical graduates must complete at least two years of graduate medical education approved by the board.

Foreign medical school graduates must have studied medicine in a school recognized by the United Nations World Health Organization (UNWHO) and have had such studies confirmed by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) Certification

Foreign medical graduates must have graduated from a legally incorporated professional school or college in good standing and completed the same post-graduate training requirements as domestic graduates

A graduate of a board-approved medical or osteopathic medical school located outside the United States or Canada may be granted a license to practice medicine in New Mexico, provided the applicant presents evidence to the board that the applicant is a person of good moral character and provided that the applicant presents satisfactory evidence to the board that the applicant has successfully passed an examination as required by the board and has successfully completed two years of postgraduate medical training in an approved postgraduate training program for physicians.

Foreign medical school graduates must submit proof of the degree of doctor of medicine or its equivalent as determined by the Board, and the standard certificate of the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates or a written statement from that Commission that the applicant passed the examination given by the Commission

Foreign medical graduates must hold certification from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates and complete 24 months of graduate medical education through the second-year level, and must demonstrate English language proficiency unless exempted

Foreign medical graduates must possess permanent ECFMG certificate or complete Fifth Pathway program; must complete minimum 3 years postgraduate residency training (or 1 year if licensed 5+ years without significant discipline); may be waived if full-time academic faculty appointment at assistant professor or higher
If diploma is from medical or osteopathic college outside United States, board may require further proof of competence by rules

International medical school graduates must provide a permanent ECFMG certificate, evidence of good moral character, citizenship or legal work authorization, and completion of a three-year post-graduate training program approved by the AMA

Foreign medical graduates must: (1) graduate from a school whose curriculum meets requirements for an unapproved medical school as determined by a committee of experts selected by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board; (2) successfully complete at least two years of approved graduate medical training in the US or Canada; (3) hold a valid ECFMG certificate; and (4) be able to communicate in English.

Foreign medical school graduates must submit current certification by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates or successor organization approved by the division; must complete one calendar year of supervised clinical training in a U.S. medical education setting accredited by LCGME; must complete postgraduate hospital training of 24 months; must pass the division's examination

Foreign medical school graduates must submit evidence of ECFMG certification and complete at least 3 years of postgraduate training in a U.S. or Canadian program accredited by an organization acceptable to the Board

Foreign medical graduates must supply evidence of: graduation from a foreign medical college credentialed by a board-approved agency; ECFMG certification; passing all steps of the USMLE; and 24 months of accredited postgraduate training.

Foreign medical graduates must hold a valid ECFMG certificate or meet alternative requirements including holding a full, unrestricted license in another state for at least 5 years with no pending disciplinary action
Foreign medical graduates must be certified by the E.C.F.M.G. (Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates) or have completed a Fifth Pathway program

fields.rationale: States cluster around whether they set an explicit day-supply ceiling, require lowest-effective-dose/evidence-based practice, delegate standard-setting to a board, restrict who or how opioids may be delegated/dispensed, protect providers acting in good faith, or restrict telemedicine prescribing specifically.

assignments.raw_value: Initial prescriptions for opioids limited to seven-day supply for adults and minors for outpatient use, with exceptions for acute medical conditions, chronic pain management, cancer pain, palliative care, logistical/travel barriers, and substance abuse treatment

Physicians may not prescribe Schedule II amphetamines and related drugs except for specific therapeutic purposes including narcolepsy, hyperkinesis, brain dysfunction, epilepsy, and clinically significant depression. Prescriptions for depression treatment are limited to 30 days unless patient is referred to a specialist.
A physician shall not be subject to disciplinary action solely for prescribing dangerous or controlled drugs for relief of chronic intractable pain; board may limit Schedule II narcotics by rule
Schedule II opioids may not be dispensed by physicians except for implantable devices or opioids for medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorders

A prescriber shall not prescribe more than a seven-day supply of an opioid to a patient who has not obtained an opioid prescription from that prescriber within the last twelve months and may exercise discretion to include a second fill for a seven-day supply. Exceptions apply for chronic pain, cancer-related pain, post-surgical pain expected to last more than fourteen days, and palliative/hospice care

When issuing a prescription for an opioid drug to an adult patient for the first time for outpatient use, a prescribing practitioner shall not issue a prescription for more than a seven-day supply of such drug. For minors, no prescription for more than a five-day supply. Exceptions apply for acute medical conditions, chronic pain, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis, or palliative care, which must be documented in the patient's medical record.

For acute pain: Schedule II opioids limited to 3-day supply, up to 7 days with documentation of medical necessity. For chronic nonmalignant pain: subject to standards of practice including treatment plans, patient agreements, and monitoring requirements

Board establishes minimum standards for prescribing controlled substances for pain management; pain management clinics are licensed and regulated; no specific statutory day-supply limit for physicians generally, but advanced practice registered nurses and physician assistants are limited to 5-day initial supply for hydrocodone/oxycodone in emergency situations
Boards must adopt rules establishing penalties for prescribing opioids in dosage amounts exceeding what would be prescribed by a reasonably prudent prescribing practitioner.
The board shall adopt guidelines for the use of controlled substances for the treatment of pain

Physicians must prescribe the lowest effective dose of an opioid and a quantity no greater than needed for the expected duration of pain, except for substance-related disorders, cancer pain, end-of-life/hospice/palliative care, or chronic pain. Dosage, quantity, and duration must be based on evidence-based clinical guidelines appropriate for the patient's age, health status, and service delivery setting.

Schedule III narcotic controlled substances and Schedule II - hydrocodone prescriptions limited to five-day supply without refill, except buprenorphine may be prescribed for up to thirty-day supply without refill for medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorders
Opioid-naive patients on outpatient basis limited to 7-day supply except for chronic pain, cancer pain, or palliative care
Opioids may only be prescribed through telemedicine if prescribed as FDA-approved medication assisted treatment for opioid use disorder or to patient in hospital or long-term care facility

Physicians may prescribe controlled substances for the treatment of intractable pain in accordance with NRS 639.23507 and 639.2391 to 639.23916, inclusive, and any regulations adopted by the State Board of Pharmacy and the Board of Medical Examiners

Physicians must comply with drug database review requirements before prescribing opioid analgesics or benzodiazepines, except in specified circumstances such as emergency treatment, hospice care, or prescriptions for 7 days or less

Physicians may only delegate prescribing of Schedule III-V controlled substances for periods not to exceed 90 days per prescription (including refills). Schedule II controlled substances may only be delegated in hospital facility-based practices for admitted patients or emergency department patients, or as part of hospice care plans. The board must adopt guidelines for prescribing opioid antagonists.

The Board shall adopt regulations for the prescribing of opioids and products containing buprenorphine with guidelines for treatment of acute pain including limitations on dosages or day supply of drugs prescribed, and for treatment of chronic pain including requirements for development of a treatment plan, an agreement for treatment signed by the provider and patient, and periodic review of treatment

A physician who discharges his or her professional obligation to relieve the pain and suffering and promote the dignity and autonomy of dying patients in his or her care and, in so doing, exceeds the average dosage of a pain relieving controlled substance, as defined in Schedules II and III of the Uniform Controlled Substance Act, does not violate this article

fields.rationale: States cluster around whether they emphasize a prior in-person visit requirement, restrictions specifically on controlled substance prescribing, cross-state licensure/jurisdiction rules, a general parity-with-in-person-care standard, or a broadly permissive framework with minimal extra restrictions.

assignments.raw_value: Physicians may prescribe controlled substances through telehealth if they comply with state and federal law governing prescription, dispensing, or administering of controlled substances. Telehealth allowed for ongoing treatment/follow-up care with established physician-patient relationship and prior in-person visit, or for life-threatening conditions with proper referral documentation

A prescription for a controlled substance may only be issued via telehealth if: (1) the telehealth visit includes synchronous audio or audio-visual communication using HIPAA compliant equipment; (2) the prescriber has had at least one in-person encounter with the patient within the preceding 12 months; and (3) the prescriber has established a legitimate medical purpose within the preceding 12 months. Exemptions apply for medical emergencies and inpatient settings.

Physicians may prescribe through telemedicine if professional relationship established; audio-only technology may not be used to renew written certification; same standard of care applies as in-person

Physicians may conduct physical or mental health status examinations through telehealth with appropriate clinical evaluation, except for certain exemptions including emergency situations and public health programs

Physicians may deliver telemedicine services in compliance with HIPAA. Telemedicine is defined as the delivery of medical services through technologies including information, electronic, and communication technologies, remote monitoring technologies, and store-and-forward transfers, to facilitate assessment, diagnosis, consultation, or treatment of a patient at an originating site while the provider is at a distant site

The provisions of section 20-9 shall apply to any individual whose practice of medicine includes any ongoing, regular or contractual arrangement whereby, regardless of residency in this or any other state, he provides, through electronic communications or interstate commerce, diagnostic or treatment services, including primary diagnosis of pathology specimens, slides or images, to any person located in this state. In the case of electronic transmissions of radiographic images, licensure shall be required for an out-of-state physician who provides, through an ongoing, regular or contractual arr

In the absence of a proper health-care provider-patient relationship, health-care providers are prohibited from issuing prescriptions solely in response to an internet questionnaire, an internet consult, or a telephone consult. A provider-patient relationship may be established via telehealth if the provider can meet the same standard of care as in-person.

A telehealth provider may not use telehealth to prescribe a controlled substance listed in Schedule II unless for psychiatric disorder treatment, inpatient hospital treatment, hospice care, or nursing home residents

A person practicing medicine via telemedicine must hold a Georgia medical license or a telemedicine license; out-of-state or foreign practitioners performing acts affecting diagnosis or treatment of Georgia patients are engaged in the practice of medicine in Georgia and must be licensed; telemedicine licensees may not practice medicine while physically present in Georgia with a patient also physically present

For opioids and cannabis, physician-patient relationship must be established after in-person consultation. For other treatments via telehealth, standards must be equivalent to traditional settings where prescribing is appropriate. Prescription based solely on online questionnaire is not acceptable standard of care.

A provider with an established provider-patient relationship may issue prescription drug orders via virtual care within the scope of the provider's license and according to applicable state and federal laws, rules, and regulations, including the Idaho community standard of care. However, the prescription drug shall not be a controlled substance unless prescribed in compliance with 21 U.S.C.

Telemedicine is defined as performance of activities including rendering written or oral opinions concerning diagnosis or treatment of a patient in Illinois by a person in a different location than the patient. Out-of-state persons providing services through telemedicine submit to Illinois jurisdiction

Providing diagnostic or treatment services to a person in Indiana when the diagnostic or treatment services are transmitted through electronic communications and are on a regular, routine, and nonepisodic basis or under an oral or written agreement to regularly provide medical services constitutes practice of medicine.

A physician holding a license issued by the applicable licensing agency of another state or who otherwise meets the requirements may practice telemedicine to treat patients located in Kansas if such physician receives a telemedicine waiver issued by the state board of healing arts. The physician must conduct an appropriate assessment and evaluation of the patient's current condition and document the appropriate medical indication for any prescription issued

Physician using telehealth must verify patient identity, establish documented diagnosis through accepted medical practices, and maintain current medical record; electronic/online/telephonic evaluation by questionnaire is inadequate for initial or follow-up evaluation

Physicians practicing telemedicine may prescribe controlled dangerous substances without an in-person examination if they hold an unrestricted license, have access to patient medical records, create medical records, and provide appropriate follow-up care. In licensed healthcare facilities, physicians may prescribe controlled substances without an in-person examination.

Physician must establish valid physician-patient relationship prior to prescribing through telemedicine, including obtaining reliable medical history, performing physical examination, having sufficient dialogue regarding treatment options, following up with patient, and maintaining contemporaneous medical record

Telemedicine practice across state lines requires licensure in Mississippi unless the evaluation, treatment and/or medical opinion is requested by a physician duly licensed to practice medicine in Mississippi who has already established a doctor-patient relationship with the patient

For physicians providing written certification of a debilitating medical condition, audio-only communication does not constitute telemedicine unless the physician has previously established a physician-patient relationship through an in-person encounter

Licensee must perform telemedicine examination or evaluation meeting requirements before prescribing medications. Opioids limited to FDA-approved medication assisted treatment or hospital/long-term care patients.

Physicians licensed in another state may be contacted via electronic or other medium for consultation with a physician licensed in Nebraska. Consultation means evaluating medical data and rendering recommendations, but does not include radiological image interpretation.

Physicians may prescribe non-opioid and opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV by means of telemedicine, with subsequent evaluation at intervals appropriate for the patient and medical condition but not less than annually, in compliance with federal and state laws. Physicians must establish a physician-patient relationship including in-person exam or telemedicine exam with identity verification, disclosure of physician information, and informed consent.

Schedule II controlled dangerous substances may be prescribed through telemedicine only after initial in-person examination and subsequent in-person visit required every three months, except for stimulants prescribed to minors under 18 with parental consent and interactive real-time audio and video

Physicians may perform acts described in the practice of medicine by using equipment that transfers information concerning the medical condition of the patient electronically, telephonically or by fiber optics, including, without limitation, through telehealth, from within or outside this State or the United States
Physicians may provide telehealth services and prescribe drugs through telehealth in accordance with standards established by the board, with equal standard of care as in-person services

Physicians may prescribe via telemedicine subject to specific requirements: Schedule II-narcotic and Schedule III-narcotic prescriptions prohibited except in hospital settings, MAT programs, palliative care/hospice, or board-approved programs; abortion-inducing drugs prohibited; must establish physician-patient relationship and comply with all state and federal laws including Prescription Monitoring Program and Ryan Haight Act

Nonresident physicians providing diagnostic or treatment services through electronic means to patients in South Dakota must be under contract with licensed health care provider, clinic, HMO, PPO, or licensed health care facility

Transfer of patient medical information to an out-of-state person not licensed in Tennessee constitutes practice of medicine if used to diagnose or treat Tennessee patients; board may issue special telemedicine licenses

A person physically located in another jurisdiction who performs an act that is part of a patient care service initiated in Texas, including acts that would affect diagnosis or treatment, is considered to be engaged in the practice of medicine in Texas and subject to board regulation. The board may adopt rules to ensure appropriate care for Medicaid and Medicare patients receiving telemedicine medical services.

A physician or podiatrist who practices medicine to a patient solely through the utilization of telemedicine technologies may not prescribe to that patient any controlled substances listed in Schedule II of the Uniform Controlled Substances Act, except for established patients or members of the same group practice. Prescribing limitations do not apply to minors with certain diagnoses or hospital patients. A physician or podiatrist may not prescribe any pain-relieving controlled substance listed in Schedule II for chronic nonmalignant pain solely based upon a telemedicine encounter, except for

fields.rationale: States cluster by how broadly PAs can prescribe controlled substances: some allow all schedules freely, some allow all schedules but with supervisory or supply constraints, some permit Schedule II only in narrow settings, some exclude Schedule II entirely, and some defer specifics to board rules.

assignments.raw_value: A licensed assistant to a physician may prescribe legend drugs to patients if the drug type, dosage, quantity prescribed, and number of refills are authorized in an approved job description signed by the supervising physician and the drug is on the formulary approved by the Board of Medical Examiners.

A physician assistant with a collaborative agreement may prescribe and dispense medication, including controlled substances, to the extent and in the manner authorized by rules promulgated by the board

A physician assistant may prescribe and administer drugs, including controlled substances in schedule IV or V in all settings, renew prescriptions for controlled substances in schedule II, III, IV or V in all settings, prescribe and administer controlled substances in schedule II or III in all settings provided the supervising physician documents approval in the patient's medical record, and prescribe and approve the use of durable medical equipment.

Physician assistants have prescriptive authority for therapeutic drugs and treatments within the scope of physician assistant practice, subject to biennial renewal. A PA working under a temporary license may not have a prescriptive practice.

A fully licensed physician assistant may prescribe or dispense any medication used in the supervising physician's practice unless listed on the formulary, including Schedule II controlled substances limited to 7-day supply

Physician assistants may be delegated authority to prescribe dangerous drugs and Schedule III, IV, or V controlled substances; may prescribe hydrocodone/oxycodone in emergency situations (5-day supply limit, patient 18+, at least 1 year post-licensure experience); cannot prescribe Schedule I or II controlled substances except as noted; authority must be contained in board-approved job description
Physician assistants may prescribe within their scope of practice under supervision; specific drug schedules determined by board rules

Physician assistants may prescribe, dispense, order, administer, or procure prescription drugs, controlled substances, or medical devices necessary to complete a course of therapy pursuant to section 148C.4.
Physician assistants have prescriptive authority as determined by the board, subject to the scope of their license and applicable state and federal laws

PA may prescribe and administer all nonscheduled legend drugs; with board approval, may prescribe Schedule III, IV, and V controlled substances to extent delegated by supervising physician; Schedule III limited to 30-day supply without refill; Schedule IV/V limited to original plus refills not exceeding 6-month supply

Physician assistants may prescribe controlled substances in Schedules III, IV, and V, and Schedule II - hydrocodone, subject to collaborative practice arrangement with supervising physician. Schedule III narcotic controlled substances and Schedule II - hydrocodone prescriptions limited to one hundred twenty-hour supply without refill
Physician assistants may prescribe and dispense schedule II through V substances and all legend drugs, subject to DEA registration and state/federal law compliance

PAs may prescribe drugs and medical devices authorized by supervising physician in written scope of practice guidelines; may prescribe Schedule II oral narcotics (initial prescription not to exceed 5-day supply) and Schedule II parenteral controlled substances in hospital settings with physician approval; subject to DEA registration and state law
Physician assistants may prescribe pursuant to protocols or collaborative agreement with a supervising physician; graduate physicians may not prescribe controlled substances

Physician assistants may prescribe nonprescription drugs, dangerous drugs, and Schedule III-V controlled substances (for up to 90 days per prescription) under a prescriptive authority agreement with a supervising physician. Schedule II controlled substances may only be prescribed in hospital facility-based practices for admitted or emergency department patients, or as part of hospice care plans.
Physician assistants may order, prescribe, procure, dispense, and administer prescription drugs, medical devices, services, and supplies, consistent with their experience, education, and training.
Physician assistants may prescribe schedule II, III, IV or V drugs but not schedule I drugs

fields.rationale: States cluster around three approaches: recognizing only ECFMG (foreign graduate pathway), recognizing only ABMS (domestic specialty boards), or recognizing ABMS alongside several other national/international boards.
